title: A founder, a billionaire and a couple with a Facebook page
lede: Titles are as given in the sources at the time. Later careers are left out where we have no source.

people.name: Norman E. Brinker
people.role: Founder; president of S&A 1966–77, chairman and chief executive 1977–83
people.text: A former Olympic equestrian who had been president of Jack in the Box. He opened Steak and Ale in February 1966, merged it with Pillsbury in 1976 and ran Pillsbury’s restaurant group, Burger King included, from June 1982.[^2][^7]
people.later: Left in July 1983 for Chili’s, which became Brinker International. Retired in 2001 and died on June 9, 2009, aged 78.[^6][^7]

people.name: Donald Slater
people.role: Chief executive of the restaurant group, 1989
people.text: Named by people involved in the March 1989 buyout as the executive who would stay in charge of Steak and Ale and Bennigan’s.[^1]

people.name: John W. Kluge
people.text: The billionaire whose private holding company owned Steak and Ale, Bennigan’s, Ponderosa and Bonanza. A reference history says he was reported to have put more than $1 billion into his steakhouses.[^3][^17]

people.name: Michael Kaufman
people.role: President, Metromedia Restaurant Group, to Sep 2003
people.text: An acquisitions specialist installed by Kluge in 1992. He announced the sale of Steak and Ale in March 2003 and stepped down six months later, saying he had commuted from New York to Dallas almost weekly for more than ten years.[^18][^23][^24]

people.name: Bob Mandes and Bill Spae
people.role: Presidents of Steak and Ale, 2000 and 2003
people.text: Mandes was president in December 2000, when the chain had 107 restaurants. Spae became chief operating officer in November 2001 and then president, and was to move to APEX with the brand.[^23][^24]

people.name: Clay Dover
people.role: Chief executive, Metromedia Restaurant Group, late 2007 – May 2008
people.text: Resigned about two months before the filing, citing differences with the owners over the company’s direction.[^5][^8]
people.later: By July 2008 he was president and chief marketing officer of Raising Cane’s Chicken Fingers.[^4]

people.name: Michelle Chow
people.text: Named in the company’s statement of July 29, 2008 as the trustee it understood would be appointed to liquidate the debtors.[^11]

people.name: Tim Gannon and Chris Sullivan
people.text: Two of the many alumni who started chains of their own, in their case Outback Steakhouse.[^25]

people.name: Paul and Gwen Mangiamele
people.role: Owners, Legendary Restaurant Brands, since Feb 2015
people.text: He became chief executive of Bennigan’s Franchising in May 2011; together they bought both brands in 2015 and spent nine years getting one Steak and Ale open.[^27][^35]

people.name: Roy Arnold
people.text: Chief executive of the Kansas company that runs the Burnsville restaurant under a 15-restaurant agreement covering several Midwestern states.[^32][^35]
